routes.description: Establish that religion, considered on balance, generates substantial humanitarian, moral, spiritual, and reconciliatory goods despite acknowledged religious harms.
routes.successCriteria: Show that religious faith distinctively motivates significant good, that its harmful forms are not exhaustive or essential, and that constructive religious practice can outweigh or materially answer the cited harms.

motionBridge.description: Religion is, on balance, a force for good in the world.

centralBridges.description: Religious belief supplies a distinctive and widespread motivation for charity, forgiveness, service, and moral self-discipline.
Religious wrongdoing is a perversion or contingent misuse of faith rather than an exhaustive measure of religion's effects.
Pluralistic and interfaith religious practice can help reconcile divided communities and support peaceful coexistence.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Belief in a higher power can foster humility, obligation, purpose, and spiritual enrichment.
Fanaticism, prejudice, and violence also arise from secular political, ethnic, and ideological sources.

routes.description: Establish that religion's supernatural authority, institutional doctrines, and exclusivist identities impose grave harms while its alleged goods remain available through secular human capacities.
routes.successCriteria: Show that religion adds unnecessary epistemic submission and divisive authority to ordinary human morality, produces serious characteristic harms, and cannot claim distinctive credit for goods achievable without it.

motionBridge.description: Religion is not, on balance, a force for good in the world.

centralBridges.description: Religion requires surrender to unsupported supernatural and human religious authority at the cost of intellectual and moral freedom.
Religious doctrine and identity intensify violence, exclusion, sexual oppression, and resistance to medicine or evidence.
Moral knowledge, charity, solidarity, and transcendent experience do not require religion, so religious institutions cannot claim unique credit for them.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Covenantal and one-true-faith claims multiply existing ethnic and political divisions.
Concrete cases such as clerical AIDS policy, Northern Ireland, Rwanda, and sectarian conflict test claims that religion is benign.

sections.title: Humanitarian work, attributable good, and countervailing harm
sections.rationale: The central comparative dispute is whether large-scale faith-based service demonstrates religion's positive balance or whether such service is non-distinctive and outweighed by doctrinal harms.

proMoves.speaker: Tony Blair
proMoves.proposition: Faith-based organizations provide extensive health care and relief, while the shared ethical essence of major faiths motivates compassion and service, making the claim that religion is unadulterated poison unsustainable.

sourceSpan.excerpt: Almost half of health care in Africa is delivered by faith-based organizations... It can also create a deep well of compassion... stimulating the impulse to do good, disciplining the propensity to be selfish and bad.

proMoves.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly introduces Blair's opening, and the uninterrupted first-person pro-motion speech is attributable to Tony Blair.

response.rationale: This is Blair's initial constructive statement of the humanitarian and motivational route and has no earlier selected target.

precisionFindings.rationale: The claim and examples are clear, and Blair acknowledges religious evil, but movement between institutional provision, individual motivation, and religion's overall balance leaves the aggregate scope partly unsettled.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The cited service figures strongly support substantial religious good, but do not by themselves establish net global balance or how much provision is causally attributable to belief.

charity.alternative: Religion can produce grave harms and religious charitable acts may also be possible through secular motivation.
charity.decisiveQualification: Blair expressly concedes that religion can be destructive while denying that those harms exhaust its effects.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The examples coherently support the existence of substantial religiously associated good, though the move compresses the bridge from existence and motivation to an on-balance conclusion.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Specific health-care proportions and organizations provide appropriate support, but causal attribution and comparative net impact remain materially underdeveloped.

responsiveness.rationale: As an opening constructive it clearly advances Blair's adopted burden and anticipates the acknowledged-harms objection.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It materially advances the central motivational bridge through direct evidence of service and stated faith-based motivation.

representationalCharity.rationale: Blair accurately concedes that religion can be destructive and does not reduce the opposing case to a denial of all religious good.

proMoves.evidenceBasis: Blair combines quantified African health-care and HIV-care claims with named Jewish, Muslim, Catholic, and local charitable examples, then identifies service to others as the shared motivating essence. His later rebuttal adds debt cancellation, schooling for girls, and care for children with HIV, but that repetition is represented by the stronger opening proposition and later reply.

conMoves.speaker: Christopher Hitchens
conMoves.proposition: Religious charity does not establish a positive balance because religious doctrine can help cause the conditions being relieved, harmful organizations also perform charity, and ordinary moral concern requires no divine source.

sourceSpan.excerpt: we'd be told about charity... Name me one religion that stands for that... AIDS was not as bad as condoms... Hamas and Hezbollah... do a great deal of charitable work. It's nothing compared to the harm that they do.

conMoves.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly gives Hitchens the rebuttal floor, and this is his uninterrupted response to Blair's opening.

components.text: Challenges the inference from charitable provision to net good by arguing that religious teaching can contribute to poverty, disease, and exclusion.
Challenges distinctive religious credit by comparing charitable activity with secular moral capacity and with harmful religious organizations that also provide aid.

response.rationale: Hitchens contacts both causal attribution and comparative balance, and explicitly states that charitable work can be outweighed by religion's harms.

precisionFindings.rationale: The counterclaim is recoverable and distinguishes charity from net impact, though its general claims about clerisy and religion range beyond the evidenced cases.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The named counterexamples warrant serious doubt about net credit, but universal language about religions opposing women's empowerment exceeds the examples supplied.

charity.alternative: Faith-based organizations can sincerely perform major charitable work and participants may experience faith as their motivation.
charity.decisiveQualification: Hitchens grants that Catholic charities and even Hamas or Hezbollah perform substantial aid, while disputing the net inference.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction between gross charitable output, causal responsibility, distinctiveness, and net impact directly exposes the opening's missing comparative bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Women's empowerment, condom doctrine, and charitable wings of militant organizations are concrete and relevant, but several broad empirical assertions are not documented or compared systematically.

responsiveness.rationale: The reply explicitly contacts the opening's decisive causal and balancing components and states why they fail to establish the conclusion.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the pro route's central claim that religious motivation establishes a positive balance.

representationalCharity.rationale: It grants substantial religious charity and sincere activity rather than denying the strongest pro evidence, while arguing that the evidence is non-dispositive.

conMoves.evidenceBasis: Hitchens contrasts charity with women's empowerment, church condom teaching, and the charitable work of Hamas and Hezbollah. His later secular-morality argument supplies a distinct nonnecessity proposition and is separately represented.

sections.title: Religious motivation versus secular moral sufficiency
sections.rationale: The parties directly contest whether faith contributes a distinctive imperative toward goodness or merely attaches supernatural authority to moral capacities already available through reason and humanism.

proMoves.speaker: Tony Blair
proMoves.proposition: Secular people can be equally good, but for vast numbers of believers faith actually supplies a distinctive imperative toward humility, forgiveness, compassion, and moral improvement.

sourceSpan.excerpt: they could easily have been inspired by humanism... But it was what led him to that... someone who is of no religious faith couldn't be just as good a person... religion can and does... give them an impulse to be better people.

proMoves.attributionBasis: This occurs in Blair's extended answer immediately before Hitchens's closing and uses explicit first-person descriptions of Blair's faith.

components.text: Concedes that nonbelievers possess moral capacity and can be equally good.
Answers nonnecessity by distinguishing logical necessity from faith's actual motivational and imperative role for believers.

response.rationale: Blair contacts both the secular-capacity premise and the inference that such capacity eliminates religious causal credit.

precisionFindings.rationale: Blair carefully limits the claim to motivation for many believers and expressly denies that believers are inherently superior.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The Omagh forgiveness account and bounded concessions support plausibility, although extrapolation to billions is asserted more broadly than evidenced.

charity.alternative: Humanism can generate the same compassion and moral conduct without religious belief.
charity.decisiveQualification: Blair fully concedes secular moral capacity and claims only that faith is an actual, sometimes stronger, motive for believers.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The necessity-versus-actual-motivation distinction is explicit and avoids claiming religious moral superiority.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The Omagh example and experiential account are relevant, but an anecdote and broad population assertion do not establish the claimed prevalence or comparative strength.

responsiveness.rationale: The move answers every indispensable part of the secular-sufficiency objection, especially the inference from alternative capacity to absence of religious contribution.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the pro route's central motivational bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: It states the secular alternative in its strongest form and expressly accepts that nonreligious people can be just as good.

proMoves.evidenceBasis: Blair acknowledges humanistic alternatives, describes prayer-inspired forgiveness after the Omagh bombing, and carefully limits his conclusion to faith's actual motivational role rather than believers' superiority.

conMoves.speaker: Christopher Hitchens
conMoves.proposition: The golden-rule insight and moral argument arise from ordinary human reason and predate the cited religions, so divine command and religious dictatorship are unnecessary for knowing right from wrong.

sourceSpan.excerpt: The injunction not to do to another what would be repulsive done to yourself is found in the Analects of Confucius... We don't require divine permission to know right from wrong... We have the reasoning and the moral suasion of Socrates and of our own abilities.

conMoves.attributionBasis: This is the concluding portion of Hitchens's clearly introduced rebuttal.

components.text: Challenges the claimed religious origin or distinctiveness of shared moral teachings by identifying prior and independent human sources.
Does not directly disprove Blair's empirical claim that faith motivates particular believers.

response.rationale: The reply diagnoses nonnecessity and explicitly concludes that divine permission and religious authority add nothing needed for moral knowledge; it does not fully answer subjective motivation.

precisionFindings.rationale: The claim is clearly limited to the nonnecessity of divine authorization for moral knowledge and argument.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The existence of recognizable nonreligious and pre-Christian moral reasoning directly warrants the nonnecessity claim, without needing to show that religion never motivates anyone.

charity.alternative: Religious teachings articulate shared moral principles and believers may regard them as motivationally authoritative.
charity.decisiveQualification: Hitchens addresses the asserted religious grounding of morality but does not deny that believers can experience religion as motivation.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Independent moral reasoning is a coherent counterexample to necessity, and the conclusion is proportionate to that counterexample.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Confucius and Socrates are apt historical counterexamples, though the move provides little documentation beyond familiar attribution.

responsiveness.rationale: The contacted source-of-morality component is decisive and the defeating consequence is explicit, while the empirical motivation component remains unanswered.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly supports the con route's central nonnecessity bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move fairly addresses religious grounding but compresses Blair's stronger claim about actual motivation into a question of moral knowledge.

conMoves.evidenceBasis: Hitchens invokes Confucian and Socratic moral reasoning and draws the narrow conclusion that people do not need divine permission or command to reason morally.

sections.title: Exclusivism, sectarian conflict, and reconciliation
sections.rationale: This section preserves the debate's strongest concrete exchange over whether religion creates or intensifies division, or can instead furnish institutions and leaders capable of reconciliation.

proMoves.speaker: Tony Blair
proMoves.proposition: Religious exclusivism is real but not essential to true religion; traditions of loving one's neighbor and examples such as cross-confessional Northern Ireland cooperation show faith can bridge divisions.

sourceSpan.excerpt: they can do and there are very many examples... Protestant Catholic churches got together... True religion is actually about embracing someone who is different... religion has tried to overcome those divides.

proMoves.attributionBasis: The moderator directs the conflict question to Blair, whose answer explicitly responds to Hitchens's preceding exclusivism argument.

components.text: Answers the claim of inherent divisiveness with interfaith teachings and a Northern Ireland reconciliation example.
Does not fully answer how one-true-church and covenantal authority claims cease to intensify group division.

response.rationale: Blair supplies relevant counterexamples and a rival account of true religion but leaves the institutional-authority mechanism materially unresolved.

precisionFindings.rationale: The reconciliation claim is clear, but 'true religion' shifts between ethical teachings, believer conduct, and an essence that excludes harmful manifestations.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Blair concedes contrary cases and offers genuine counterexamples, but those examples do not establish that reconciliatory religion predominates.

charity.alternative: Religious identities and exclusive truth claims can deepen preexisting political and ethnic conflict.
charity.decisiveQualification: Blair concedes many such cases while denying that exclusivism is religion's sole or authentic expression.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Counterexamples defeat an absolute divisiveness claim, but defining constructive practice as true religion risks insulating the central essence claim from adverse cases.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Northern Ireland and cross-tradition teachings are relevant, but the examples are selective and the historical causal role of religion is not compared.

responsiveness.rationale: The reply contacts the decisive claim with genuine counterexamples but does not resolve Hitchens's mechanism involving exclusive supernatural authority.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It materially advances the central coexistence bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: Blair explicitly accepts that faith can deepen conflict and states the objection accurately before offering a bounded contrary case.

proMoves.evidenceBasis: Blair cites Protestant and Catholic leaders cooperating in Northern Ireland, shared neighbor-love teachings, early Islamic science and women's rights, and faith-driven cross-divide work. The strongest causal limitation remains his reliance on 'true religion.'

proMoves.speaker: Tony Blair
proMoves.proposition: Rwanda, Northern Ireland, and the Middle East have tribal and political causes alongside religious ones, while religious actors have both harmed and protected people; these cases therefore do not justify condemning religion as a whole.

sourceSpan.excerpt: it really would be bizarre to say that the conflict in Rwanda was a result of the Catholic Church... members... stood up and protected and died alongside people... politics of the situation... not only religion.

proMoves.attributionBasis: The moderator directly returns the floor to Blair, and Blair answers Hitchens's Rwanda and Northern Ireland examples.

components.text: Contacts the concession that conflicts have nonreligious ethnic, colonial, and political causes.
Does not rebut the narrower claim that pulpits and religious identity materially intensified violence even when they were not sole causes.

response.rationale: Blair provides substantial contrary causal context but mainly answers a sole-cause claim that Hitchens expressly disavowed.

precisionFindings.rationale: The multicausal claim and concessions are clear, and Blair does not claim religion played no role.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The political and tribal factors are relevant, but calling a Catholic-causation claim bizarre overstates the answer to Hitchens's narrower intensification argument.

charity.alternative: Religion need not be the sole cause of a conflict to intensify it through pulpits, identity, and supernatural sanction.
charity.decisiveQualification: Hitchens expressly conceded ethnic and colonial causes in Rwanda while alleging religious amplification.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The multicausal reasoning is sound against monocausal attribution, but it does not entail that religion's contribution is minor or outweighed.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Blair supplies concrete alternative causes and religious rescuers, though without comparative evidence about their magnitude against clerical complicity.

responsiveness.rationale: The reply addresses secondary causal context but leaves the decisive intensification component unanswered.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It attacks the con route's subsidiary counterexample bridge and must remain within the subsidiary band.

representationalCharity.rationale: Blair acknowledges part of Hitchens's position but weakens it toward the claim that Rwanda was simply caused by the Catholic Church.

proMoves.evidenceBasis: Blair distinguishes tribal, colonial, national, and political causes; acknowledges badly behaving clergy; cites religious rescuers; and disputes the inference from examples to a whole-religion verdict.

conMoves.speaker: Christopher Hitchens
conMoves.proposition: Monotheistic covenant and one-true-church claims turn faith into a force multiplier for ethnic and political division, making common humanism harder rather than easier.

sourceSpan.excerpt: an expression of exclusivism. This is our God... the one true church... faith is a fantastic force multiplier... of all things that are in fact divisive rather than inclusive.

conMoves.attributionBasis: The moderator directs the globalization and shared-values question to Hitchens, and the answer is an uninterrupted con-side argument.

response.rationale: Within the selected ledger this is the first discrete formulation of the exclusivism mechanism and is treated as a constructive.

precisionFindings.rationale: The force-multiplier claim is clear and qualified with 'very often,' but it ranges from specific monotheistic forms to faith generally.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Named church claims and sectarian examples warrant an intensification mechanism, but the generalization to any faith exceeds the supplied comparison.

charity.alternative: Shared religious values and interfaith practice can unite people around common service and human dignity.
charity.decisiveQualification: Hitchens recognizes the desired goal as common humanism but argues that supernatural exclusivity obstructs it.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The mechanism from exclusive sacred identity to intensified division is intelligible and supported by examples, with some overextension from particular traditions.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Catholic exclusivity, Balkan identity, Lebanon, and Yugoslavia are specific evidence, though representativeness and independent political causes remain compressed.

responsiveness.rationale: As a constructive it squarely advances the adopted burden and engages the shared-values premise motivating the issue.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly supports the declared subsidiary exclusivism bridge and remains within that tier's band.

representationalCharity.rationale: It preserves the pro aspiration toward common humanism but gives limited treatment to nonexclusive or reformist religious forms.

conMoves.evidenceBasis: Hitchens identifies covenantal tribal identity, the Catholic one-true-church claim, Balkan religious-national identity, and sectarian wars as evidence for the intensification mechanism.

conMoves.speaker: Christopher Hitchens
conMoves.proposition: The fact that religious leaders later bridge conflict does not erase religion's role in producing or intensifying the divide, as illustrated by Northern Ireland and clerical participation in the Rwandan genocide.

sourceSpan.excerpt: where does the religious divide come from?... Rwanda... the Hutu power genocide... was preached from the pulpits... not entirely the fault of religion... it does tend to make it very very much worse.

conMoves.attributionBasis: The moderator invites Hitchens to respond, and he directly addresses Blair's Northern Ireland example before moving to Rwanda.

components.text: Challenges the inference from later religious reconciliation by asking whether the same identities and institutions helped constitute the original divide.
Concedes nonreligious ethnic and colonial causes while alleging that religious preaching materially amplified violence.

response.rationale: Hitchens directly contacts the reconciliation example, supplies a causal-baseline objection, and explicitly states the defeating consequence that religion made conflicts worse.

precisionFindings.rationale: The move carefully disclaims the claim that religion wholly caused Rwanda and instead argues material intensification.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The examples support possible and plausible amplification, but some factual allegations are asserted without documentation and their relative causal magnitude is not established.

charity.alternative: Church leaders can cross religious divides and play a constructive role in peace processes.
charity.decisiveQualification: Hitchens accepts the later bridging activity but argues that it must be evaluated against religion's contribution to the antecedent divide.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The baseline and counterfactual objection directly limits the evidential value of reconciliation after religiously marked conflict.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Northern Ireland and Rwanda are concrete and causally relevant, but several institutional allegations and comparative magnitudes require verification.

responsiveness.rationale: It directly contacts the strongest reconciliation example, incorporates its qualification, and states why it does not establish the pro conclusion.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the pro route's central coexistence bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: Hitchens expressly grants that religion was not the entire cause and acknowledges the claimed bridging before presenting the baseline objection.

conMoves.evidenceBasis: Hitchens contrasts centuries of Christian identification in Northern Ireland with later bridge-building, then uses Rwanda while explicitly conceding ethnic differences and colonial influence.

sections.title: Supernatural authority, freedom, and spiritual purpose
sections.rationale: The closing exchange crystallizes the deepest route conflict: whether allegiance to transcendent authority disciplines human will toward good or exacts an unacceptable sacrifice of reason and autonomy.

proMoves.speaker: Tony Blair
proMoves.proposition: Faith in a higher power need not produce servitude or certainty; it can acknowledge ignorance, coexist with science, discipline human will, and direct believers toward the best of humanity.

sourceSpan.excerpt: those who want to suppress freedom... are not confined to... religious faith... faith is not about certainty... awareness of my own ignorance... not... imprisoned by that superior will... discipline and use our own will.

proMoves.attributionBasis: This is Blair's formally introduced closing statement and explicitly responds to Hitchens's immediately preceding freedom argument.

components.text: Rejects the claim that transcendent obedience necessarily feels or functions as servitude, offering humility and self-discipline as an alternative account.
Does not answer the claim that organized religion requires fallible human interpreters endowed with divine authority.
Acknowledges uncertainty but does not supply evidence for the higher power whose authority grounds the obligation.

response.rationale: Blair answers the servitude characterization at the experiential and ethical level but leaves institutional mediation and evidential warrant substantially untouched.

precisionFindings.rationale: The humility and discipline thesis is recoverable, but 'meaning,' 'purpose,' and 'higher power' remain broad and partly unspecified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Blair explicitly distinguishes faith from scientific certainty and frames the conclusion personally, matching the limited experiential warrant.

charity.alternative: Obedience to supernatural and clerical authority sacrifices intellectual and moral freedom.
charity.decisiveQualification: Blair addresses the objection as a claim about what obedience does to agency, but not its strongest institutional-interpreter component.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction between disciplined and extinguished will is coherent, though the inference from higher power to beneficial discipline remains asserted.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move relies mainly on personal belief, an Einstein attribution, and experiential interpretation rather than independent support for the claimed higher power or causal effect.

responsiveness.rationale: It directly contacts the autonomy component but leaves the human-interpreter and evidential components unanswered.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the con route's central authority bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: Blair recognizes the servitude objection but narrows it toward subjective experience and does not fully represent the institutional-authority challenge.

proMoves.evidenceBasis: Blair contrasts religious and secular fanaticism, distinguishes faith from scientific certainty, acknowledges ignorance, and describes obedience as disciplining rather than imprisoning human will.

conMoves.speaker: Christopher Hitchens
conMoves.proposition: Even movements with heroic works are not worth the sacrifice of freedom demanded by infallible authority; religion similarly requires supernatural belief and submission to human interpreters claiming divine authority.

sourceSpan.excerpt: There was real heroism... but we opposed it... not worth the sacrifice of freedom... place yourself under an infallible leadership... religion means that you will have to follow someone... this person has divine authority.

conMoves.attributionBasis: This is Hitchens's formally introduced closing statement and explicitly returns to Blair's preceding account of transcendence and obligation.

components.text: Concedes that belief systems can inspire heroic and compassionate conduct.
Argues that good works do not justify the distinct cost of infallible supernatural and institutional authority.

response.rationale: The communist analogy concedes motivational goods, identifies submission as the defect, and explicitly concludes that the cost makes the package unacceptable.

precisionFindings.rationale: The cost argument is clear, but the categorical claim that religion necessarily entails following a divinely authorized leader overgeneralizes across religious forms.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The institutional argument is powerful against hierarchical traditions, but the universal necessity claim is not warranted for every form of religion or individualized faith.

charity.alternative: Faith can genuinely inspire humility, forgiveness, compassion, and heroic service without extinguishing agency.
charity.decisiveQualification: Hitchens expressly grants heroic works and high motives, then argues that they do not offset the authority cost.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The analogy cleanly separates beneficial outputs from unacceptable authority costs, but its universal bridge from religion to infallible leadership is materially broad.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Communist institutional history and Catholic hierarchy illustrate the mechanism, but they do not establish necessity across religion as a whole.

responsiveness.rationale: The move grants Blair's strongest motivational premise and directly states why it fails to establish an acceptable or net-good institution.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly supports the con route's central authority bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: It represents the pro case at its strongest by conceding heroic conduct, dignity, and sincere motivation before contesting the price.

conMoves.evidenceBasis: Hitchens develops the communist analogy at length, explicitly credits heroic adherents, then identifies infallible leadership, supernatural claims, and clerical interpretation as the unacceptable additional commitments.

pro.rationale: No distinct debate-wide completion consequence remains outside the selected moves, response links, importance judgments, section weights, and ratings.

eligibility.completionCriterion: No separate criterion qualifies beyond whether the pro route establishes distinctive religious good sufficient for an on-balance conclusion.
eligibility.distinctConsequence: None; the incomplete net-balance bridge and the strength of religious motivation are already captured in the selected moves and section structure.
eligibility.counterfactual: Removing the already-scored limitations would change move and section judgments rather than create an independent adjustment consequence.

con.rationale: No distinct debate-wide completion consequence survives the duplicate-exclusion rule; authority, harm, nonnecessity, and conflict amplification are represented directly.

eligibility.completionCriterion: No separate criterion qualifies beyond whether characteristic religious harms and authority costs outweigh the acknowledged goods.
eligibility.distinctConsequence: None; the remaining generalization and comparative-balance gaps are already reflected in move warrants, calibration findings, and section coverage.
eligibility.counterfactual: If the con generalizations and net comparison were fully established, the selected move ratings would change; there is no additional debate-wide consequence to add.
